section_summary: This section combines early-1945 proposals and directives for coordinating American collection of Japanese intelligence in Europe with a detailed SHAEF assessment of Japanese personnel, organizations, communications, and suspected espionage in France and Switzerland. It then shifts to 1946: a Stockholm telegram discusses the possible interrogation of former military attaché Makoto Onodera, while the opening portion of a Strategic Services Unit study reconstructs Japanese wartime intelligence operations in Stockholm and Helsinki. Recurring concerns include Allied coordination, French protection or surveillance of Japanese nationals, Swiss-based intelligence networks, and Japanese collaboration with Polish, Finnish, Baltic, German, Hungarian, and Swedish sources.

subfiles.title: Letter proposing a London center for Japanese intelligence
subfiles.about: Reber recommends establishing a London center to coordinate State Department reporting and operations concerning Japanese activities in Europe.
subfiles.summary: Reber agrees with Hornbeck and Allison to create a London Japanese-intelligence center with Allison as director and Pell as liaison; forwards memoranda, the SHAEF directive and Abbott's report.

subfiles.title: Letter endorsing coordinated Japanese-intelligence work in Europe
subfiles.about: Hornbeck conditionally endorses the proposed London-centered organization and urges stronger Allied action toward Japanese activities in France and Belgium.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck agrees Allison should coordinate Japanese intelligence in Europe and Pell field operations, conditional on staffing and continuity; criticizes weak handling in France and Belgium.

subfiles.title: Coordination of Japanese Intelligence
subfiles.about: Allison sets out the staffing, authority, liaison, and familiarization requirements for directing a Japanese-intelligence organization in London.
subfiles.summary: Allison asks to be relieved of unrelated duties, requests formal recognition by War, Navy and British authorities, and suggests spending days at SHAEF.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on postwar Japanese counterintelligence in Europe
subfiles.to: Samuel Reber and Robert D. Murphy
subfiles.about: Pell argues that the United States needs a permanent, centrally directed Army-Navy-State system for Japanese counterintelligence in Europe.
subfiles.summary: Pell warns Japan is preparing a postwar European intelligence network centered in Zurich and urges including Japanese counterintelligence in Control Council machinery and a coordinating center, possibly at The Hague.

subfiles.title: Intelligence Directive No. 24: Directive on Handling of Japanese Intelligence
subfiles.from: Walter Bedell Smith, authenticated by Kenneth W. D. Strong
subfiles.to: Allied intelligence staffs and T forces in the European theater
subfiles.about: SHAEF directs the identification, interrogation, safeguarding, analysis, reproduction, and dissemination of Japanese intelligence targets and documents found in Europe.
subfiles.summary: Intelligence Directive No. 24 creates a Japanese Intelligence Section in SHAEF G-2, defines targets and requires safeguarding and forwarding documents for analysis.

subfiles.title: Cover memorandum on Japanese activities in Europe
subfiles.to: Intelligence Officer, Commander, U.S. Naval Forces in Europe
subfiles.about: Abbott forwards his broader assessment of Japanese activities in Europe and notes the difficulty of maintaining coverage in Switzerland.
subfiles.summary: Abbott transmits a report and French documents on the Japanese consulate at Marseille, limiting distribution to protect sources; neither US nor Britain had naval representation in Switzerland.

subfiles.title: Japanese Activities in Europe: Estimate of the Situation
subfiles.to: Head, Counter-Intelligence Sub-Division, G-2 Division, SHAEF
subfiles.about: Abbott assesses official and covert Japanese activity in liberated France and Switzerland, incorporating French documents, source reports, personnel lists, and Robert Pell’s Swiss field investigation.
subfiles.summary: The report finds French policy toward Japanese nationals hesitant and inconsistent: military-security searches in Paris were obstructed by Swiss diplomatic protection, officials contemplated releasing detained consular personnel, and suspected Japanese agents or sympathizers often received lenient treatment. It documents Japanese residents and commercial organizations in Paris and Marseille, alleged espionage communications, and French plans for telephone surveillance. Pell’s embedded report identifies Switzerland—especially Bern, Geneva, and Zurich—as a major Japanese communications and intelligence center, describes diplomatic, financial, military, naval, and press covers, and supplies extensive personnel lists. Abbott recommends further research and distribution of the report and accompanying microfilm to U.S. military, naval, and State Department authorities.

subfiles.title: Telegram concerning possible interrogation of General Onodera
subfiles.from: Christian M. Ravndal, U.S. Legation Stockholm
subfiles.about: The Stockholm legation reports French interest in detaining and interrogating Makoto Onodera while his repatriation party crosses Germany en route to Naples.
subfiles.summary: French counterintelligence sought to question Onodera on information allegedly supplied by Garnier; the US legation urged his continuing to Naples, with options up to detaining him in the American zone.

subfiles.title: Dissemination Branch transmittal to Jack D. Neal
subfiles.from: Chief, Dissemination Branch, Strategic Services Unit
subfiles.about: The Strategic Services Unit forwards attached intelligence material to a State Department official.
subfiles.summary: Dissemination Branch cover sheet sending material DB-1225 to Jack Neal.

subfiles.title: Japanese Wartime Intelligence Activities in Northern Europe
subfiles.about: The opening portion of an SSU study reconstructs the organization, objectives, finances, communications, sources, and security methods of Japanese military intelligence in Stockholm and Helsinki.
subfiles.summary: Based chiefly on 1946 interrogations of Makoto Onodera, Hiroshi Onouchi, and their associates, the study describes long-term Japanese Army collaboration with Polish, Finnish, Estonian, and Latvian intelligence against the Soviet Union and later the Western Allies. It traces how Stockholm evolved into a major Japanese espionage post, outlines the personnel and directives of the Stockholm and Helsinki military-attaché offices, and explains their budgets, courier systems, cables, and limited clandestine wireless links. The study emphasizes Onodera’s use of foreign General Staff organizations, personal obligations, financial assistance, and contacts such as Rybikowski, Maasing, Hallamaa, Petersen, and Kraemer. Pages 35-46 end during the discussion of counterintelligence, penetration agents, and attempted deception operations, so the study continues beyond this section.
